raw_text:
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) reduce sudden cardiac death in selected patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and systolic heart failure, but conventional transvenous systems expose patients to venous access complications, endovascular infection, tricuspid-valve interaction, and chronic lead failure [1,2]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillation while eliminating intravascular and intracardiac hardware. The system consists of a lateral thoracic pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode; it senses a subcutaneous electrogram and delivers high-energy transthoracic shocks. Its principal trade-off is the absence of chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), and antitachycardia pacing (ATP), although short post-shock pacing is available.

Early human studies established feasibility and high defibrillation efficacy [3]. The pivotal IDE trial demonstrated that S-ICD implantation was achievable in most screened patients, met prespecified safety and efficacy end points, and successfully converted spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, although inappropriate shocks were relatively common in early experience [4]. Subsequent registries broadened the evidence base. EFFORTLESS showed reproducible performance in real-world practice [5], pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS data confirmed high final shock efficacy and low rates of systemic infection or electrode failure [6], and the full EFFORTLESS cohort demonstrated acceptable mid-term complication and shock outcomes [7]. Five-year EFFORTLESS follow-up showed durable conversion efficacy, modest need for later transvenous conversion for pacing indications, and continued absence of the classic endovascular lead-failure phenotype [8]. The U.S. post-approval study and UNTOUCHED extended these findings to larger and more contemporary cohorts, including many primary-prevention heart-failure patients with low ejection fraction and standardized high-rate, dual-zone programming [9,10].

Randomized comparisons have clarified the clinical niche of the S-ICD. In PRAETORIAN, S-ICD therapy was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks among patients without pacing indications [11]. ATLAS, enriched for younger or lead-complication-prone patients, showed fewer perioperative major lead-related complications with the S-ICD without a clear loss of shock effectiveness [12]. Secondary PRAETORIAN analyses suggest that lead-related complications, systemic infections, and invasive reinterventions are less frequent or less severe with S-ICD than with transvenous systems [13]. However, an individual participant-data meta-analysis of PRAETORIAN and ATLAS reported that first inappropriate shocks were infrequent but more common with S-ICD, driven mainly by cardiac oversensing and noncardiac signals, whereas atrial-arrhythmia-related inappropriate shocks favored the S-ICD [14].

Patient selection remains central. Ideal candidates have a standard ICD indication, no need for bradycardia pacing, CRT, or likely ATP-responsive recurrent monomorphic VT, and a strong reason to avoid transvenous leads: young age, difficult venous access, prior device infection, dialysis, congenital or inherited disease, or anticipated long device lifetime. Preimplant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory because T-wave oversensing and low QRS/T ratios can make sensing unreliable [15]. Algorithm-based screening may increase eligible vectors [16], and exercise screening is particularly useful in dynamic phenotypes such as Brugada syndrome or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, where repolarization changes can emerge at higher heart rates [17]. Ambulatory and repeat screening studies underscore that eligibility is not static and that morphology can vary with posture, exertion, and disease progression [30].

Implant technique has evolved. The two-incision technique reduces dissection and eliminates the superior parasternal incision [18]. Intermuscular generator placement between serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi improves cosmesis, stabilizes the can, reduces fat between the shocking vector and thorax, and may reduce pocket discomfort or high impedance [19]. Comparative contemporary experience supports intermuscular approaches as part of best practice [20]. Defibrillation testing has historically been recommended because the S-ICD shock vector is extrathoracic and positioning-dependent; observational studies and reviews suggest high success rates, but the necessity of routine testing in all patients remains debated [25–27].

The main device-specific adverse event is inappropriate shock. Early episodes were dominated by T-wave oversensing and sometimes mitigated by vector reprogramming, exercise template acquisition, or zone changes [21,22]. Later series identified myopotential noise, QRS undersensing with automatic gain changes, atrial arrhythmias, and first-generation algorithms as additional mechanisms [23]. Broader meta-analysis shows inappropriate shock rates have declined over time with improved screening, dual-zone programming, higher rate cutoffs, delayed therapy, and sensing filters [24]. When transvenous lead malfunction occurs in patients without pacing requirements, lead abandonment or extraction followed by S-ICD implantation is an emerging strategy, but it requires individualized discussion of abandoned-lead risk, infection history, venous access, and future pacing probability [29].

In summary, the S-ICD is a mature alternative to the transvenous ICD for patients needing defibrillation but not pacing. Its strongest advantage is avoidance of endovascular lead morbidity; its main limitations are lack of ATP/CRT and sensing-related inappropriate shocks. Contemporary outcomes are best when careful screening, modern programming, meticulous intermuscular implantation, and shared decision-making are integrated into patient selection.
